audience: UI developers, UX designers, and people building AI features
topics: React, Solid, Qwik, Next.js, Gatsby, and Remix
Native browser APIs as alternatives to dependencies, with practical tradeoffs
New browser APIs, their support status, and progressive enhancement
AI tools and techniques for building user interfaces
UX design and how it is evolving with AI
UX patterns for applications with AI features
UI bugs, reproducible examples, root causes, and fixes
voice: Clear, practical, specific, and conversational. Explain one useful idea at a time.

post_style.opening: Lead with a concrete UI, accessibility, AI, or UX problem and why it matters.
structure: Explain the concept in short paragraphs
Choose either a code walkthrough or an informational explainer based on the subject
For code walkthroughs, show anti-patterns and corrected examples
For informational posts, explain what changed, how it works, benefits, limitations, and implications without requiring code
Give practical takeaways, limitations, and a short checklist
End with a relevant question or takeaway, then focused hashtags
post_style.formatting: Use short lines, clear section labels, restrained check/cross markers, and plain-text code that remains readable without syntax highlighting.
post_style.adapt_to_topic: For non-code AI or UX topics, use contrasting interface behaviors or user journeys instead of forcing code examples.
post_style.hashtags: Use a small set of relevant technical and audience hashtags.
post_style.visual_role: Summarize or demonstrate the post; keep the key lesson readable at a glance.

freshness.guidance: Prefer developments from the last 30 days. Older fundamentals are useful only with a specific current application, newly relevant tradeoff, or recent change. Avoid generic introductions and recycled basics. Never invent novelty or a publication date to pass this policy.
freshness.evidence: Include a primary-source URL, a verified development date when available, and an explanation of what the audience learns now. Undated or older developments require explicit review notes; no unsupported claims of being new.
freshness.skip_when: If research yields no useful current angle, stop with an explanation instead of filling the queue with stale material.

animate_when: Demonstrating an interaction, focus movement, or UI bug and its fix
Showing a sequence, state transition, or AI response lifecycle
Comparing before and after behavior where motion explains the difference
infographics.motion_guidance: Use a short, readable sequence with deliberate pauses. Avoid flashing and decorative motion. Include a useful static summary and alternative text.
infographics.reference_style: Keep diagram labels and layout visible while moving markers or highlights along connections to explain a sequence. Use before/after panels and labeled flows where appropriate; use original artwork and the owner's branding.
infographics.approval: Preview the complete animation, final post, and static fallback together. Any correction to any asset requires a new approval version.
infographics.publishing: Verify animated GIF support for the actual LinkedIn API path before selecting the published asset. Never silently replace an approved asset; request approval for a different format.

posting_schedule.publishing: Publish only after approval of the exact post and infographic.

custom_topics.weekly_cadence: Custom requests are additional; do not replace or reschedule the three weekly requests.
custom_topics.approval: Use the same research, infographic, correction, and first-valid-response approval workflow.
custom_topics.topic_scope: Owner-supplied topics may extend beyond the usual topic list. Preserve the requested subject and angle; do not silently substitute another topic.
custom_topics.freshness: Apply the same factual and timeliness review. Flag an older topic honestly and look for a useful current application; never manufacture novelty.
